title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
description: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The US se
body: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in GloucestershireByHafsa Khalil and Daniel SandfordUK correspondentUpdated 28 minutes agoA US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police. Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to. "We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.Image source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested on 10 November On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress.""These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners."Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said. "This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take."Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody

title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
description: Image source, LionsgateImage caption, Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16ByIan YoungsCulture reporterReviews of the latest Hunger Ga
body: Image source, LionsgateImage caption, Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16ByIan YoungsCulture reporterReviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, Ralph Fiennes stars as President SnowSunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes."This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external."It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar FlickermanThe film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't."In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekendHowever, the Hollywood Reporter, external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."And Time Out's four-star review, external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

schema.headline: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'

title: Peter Storey: Former Arsenal and England midfielder dies aged 81
description: Former Arsenal and England midfielder Peter Storey has died at the age of 81.Storey made 501 appearances in all competitions for the Gunners between 1
body: Former Arsenal and England midfielder Peter Storey has died at the age of 81.Storey made 501 appearances in all competitions for the Gunners between 1965 and 1977, scoring 17 goals.He was part of the Double-winning Arsenal team which secured the First Division title and FA Cup in 1970-71 under manager Bertie Mee."Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of double winner Peter Storey," Arsenal said in a statement."All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time."We will pay our respects to Peter at our forthcoming home match against Borussia Dortmund."Surrey-born Storey joined Arsenal as an apprentice in 1961 and made his first-team debut against Leicester City in 1965, initially starting his career at right-back before being moved into midfield.He is currently eighth on Arsenal's list of all-time appearance holders and was capped 19 times by England, although he did not feature in a major tournament for the Three Lions.Storey collected runners-up medals with Arsenal in the League Cup in 1967-68 and 1968-69 and in the FA Cup in 1971-72. He joined Second Division Fulham on a free transfer in March 1977 and made 19 appearances for the Cottagers before his contract was terminated later that year and he retired.However, Storey had something of a troubled life after his retirement from professional football.He was convicted of running a brothel - for which he received a suspended prison sentence in 1979 - and was later jailed for three years for his involvement in a counterfeiting operation, then served another prison sentence in 1990 for attempting to smuggle pornographic videos into Britain.

schema.headline: Peter Storey: Former Arsenal and England midfielder dies aged 81

title: William and Catherine celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
description: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winner
body: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow."The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

schema.headline: William and Catherine celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai

title: Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's ideas help you?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterAlan Milburn has said the country needs a "complete system reset" to bring down the number
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterAlan Milburn has said the country needs a "complete system reset" to bring down the number of young people not in work or education - known as "Neets".In a major review, published on Tuesday,, external he suggested a raft of proposals to address the problem, which mostly cover England but he says can be adapted in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.Each of his recommendations will need to be accepted by the government and implemented and paid for before they become reality - and that could take some time. So how might today's proposals affect you if you are Neet?A new Youth Opportunity ServiceAt the heart of the recommendations, Milburn says, is a new Youth Opportunity Service. He wants this to be implemented locally, with each area drawing up a plan to help their own young people.It would bring together employment, careers, health and practical support, with each young person getting a named adviser and a personalised plan.Milburn wants areas to begin building their Youth Opportunity Service from 2027, with one in place everywhere by the end of 2029.Within 14 days of entering the service, a young person would then meet with a named adviser. Within four weeks, they would have their "personalised participation plan", setting out what both the support services and the young person involved would do, and when.Jobs wise, Milburn wants there to be initiatives like work placements of up to 12 weeks, structured volunteering opportunities, and help to create businesses.He also wants those who remain Neet - despite enagaging with support - to be provided with a paid six-month job, funded by the government.The government has already committed to a legal guarantee of job support in theory, but the exact workings still need to be worked out.More apprenticeships and college placesAlongside more work opportunities, Milburn wants a "major expansion" in further education for 18- to 24 year-olds, as well as more apprenticeship places.Over the next decade, he wants the number of young people completing an apprenticeship to double, and for apprenticeships to rival university as an option for school leavers.Colleges should also get new funding for participation and work-readiness, the review says, initially targeted at 16- and 17-year-olds who are Neet or at serious risk of becoming so.He also wants the government to develop new industry-led technical colleges and specialist campuses.If the reforms are enacted, Milburn says young people should have better access to high-quality further education and apprenticeships by 2028.Under the proposals, schools, colleges and universities would be judged by whether pupils make successful transitions into further learning and work, rather than just academic achievements.By 2036, he wants 35% of each year group to have started a high-quality apprenticeship by age 25.More mental health supportMilburn has said he wants a fundamental transformation of how mental health support for young people is delivered.Young people who are Neet should be guaranteed fast-track access to services within three months, according to his recommendations. This would include things like vocational rehabilitation, talking therapies and counselling as part of a young person's plan with their local Youth Opportunity Service - which would be rolled out between 2027 and 2029 under the plans.There has been a big rise in mental distress among children and young people in recent years, and Milburn's report comes at a time the NHS is facing huge pressures.Milburn wants mental health support to be available for all young people digitally, without needing a diagnosis.Some areas are already using these approaches, but scaling them up would be a major challenge and would take a long time to introduce across the board.Plus, Milburn wants "fitness to work" notes to be taken out of the hands of GPs and put into community work and health teams, and for them to be "a trigger for help - not simply a certificate of absence".Milburn wants these changes to begin in 2027 and would be linked to the Youth Opportunity Service rollout, which would be complete by 2029 under the plans.More incentives for employers to hire young peopleMilburn has said he wants companies to be incentivised to employ more young people, with the report highlighting a competitive jobs market and applicants who often fail to hear back from potential employers.The report includes three asks of employers: to create more genuine first jobs, more first-job apprenticeships and much wider access to meaningful work experience.Plus, Milburn wants large employers to find ways of responding to rejected job applicants.These changes should be felt by both employers and the young people looking for jobs by 2029, the report says.To achieve this, the report suggests a £3,000 payment for employers who take on someone who has been Neet for six months, with a further premium of £2,000 available if they are a small business.An extra payment of £2,000 would go to employers taking on somebody taking substantially greater barriers, such as care leavers or disabled young people.These payments are proposed to be part of changes to the Youth Jobs Grant - which already exists, external - but they would expand under Milburn's proposals from 2027.Get in touchShare your experiences and ask your questions.

schema.headline: Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's ideas help you?

title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
description: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv a
body: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya AbishevBBC News RussianUpdated 1 hour agoUkraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014. The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.Image source, Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesImage caption, Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands."We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."Image caption, Images show the damage to the Crimean Bridge from the overnight attackThe damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.  Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry. Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.Figure caption, Watch: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attackIn Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

schema.headline: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
description: ByNick Edser and Simon BrowningBusiness reportersUpdated 7 hours agoLowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24,
body: ByNick Edser and Simon BrowningBusiness reportersUpdated 7 hours agoLowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals.Costs the key issueImage caption, Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staffCutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience."My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says."In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise  the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".Cash incentivesImage caption, Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away"Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.Image caption, Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us."He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.Guaranteed hours a concernOne of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report.Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work.Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year.Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.'The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure.It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue.Help getting staffImage source, Dean GreeneYoung people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff."We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role."There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.Get in touchShare your experiences and ask your questions.

schema.headline: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?

title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterHe has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterHe has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between."I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.'Bring the weird'Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external."Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external."Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external."About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."Image source, A24/Moviestore/ShutterstockImage caption, Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17."Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries"."He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?TenetImage source, Warner Bros/Everett/ShutterstockImage caption, Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit."He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away."Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet."For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."The BatmanImage source, Getty ImagesNew York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external."Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin."Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.The OdysseyImage source, Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/ShutterstockAlthough Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle."I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says."What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond."All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote."Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware."Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations. "Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."PrimetimeImage source, A24Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero."He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains."It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."Dune: Part ThreeImage source, Warner Bros PicturesPattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve. The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond."The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced."He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

schema.headline: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007

title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterUpdated 12:35 GMTIf you're one of the nearly one millio
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterUpdated 12:35 GMTIf you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out.Where are the available jobs?Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.It used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.Some people live in one area and work in another, but the analysis did not account for this.Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs?Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.What are the typical rates of pay?Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.How many job vacancies are there overall?While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers.Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.Get in touchShare your experiences and ask your questions.

schema.headline: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?

title: Oxford protest against talk by academic who made Arday plagiarism claim
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into Oriel CollegeUpdated
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into Oriel CollegeUpdated 3 hours agoHundreds of people have gathered to protest against a talk at an Oxford University college by the academic who accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism.Stand Up To Racism organised a demonstration against Nathan Cofnas's talk at Oriel College, organised by Oxford Reform UK, on Tuesday evening.Protesters, some with face masks on, appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into the college before the talk.Dozens of protesters held signs saying "Nathan Cofnas not welcome" and "Remember Professor Jason Arday".Chants of "Nathan Cofnas shut him down" could be heard.Cofnas, who has advocated for "race realism", wrote a blog accusing Prof Arday of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis.Image source, Nathan CofnasImage caption, Confas's talk was entitled "Is DEI (diversity, equality and inclusion) Undermining Higher Education?"It prompted a weeks-long plagiarism row that saw 41-year-old Arday face intense public scrutiny about his work and other achievements.Although he denied the allegations made against him, Arday resigned his post as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education. He was found dead at his home in south London on 14 August.Theo Biggs, 20, who is a student at nearby Oxford Brookes University, said: "Oxford University is a prestigious university, and what is talked about here is talked about around the world."Giving this sort of conversation a platform is legitimising it essentially."A course administrator at the university, who did not want to be named, said: "I've seen a lot of students of colour are feeling unwelcome, uncomfortable, frightened by the fact that Oriel and the wider university has not shut this down."Another student added: "I've worked really hard to get here. I pay a lot of money to be here, and then me being a minority is like the biggest sin in the world. It's not something I want, it's not something I'm standing for at all."Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor after the allegations of plagiarism that he deniedThe talk's event page stated Cofnas "faced recent controversy after exposing the plagiarism of Jason Arday".Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.He was suspended from Ghent University in Belgium in August before being reinstated after pressure by US ambassador Bill White.On Thursday, protesters against the talk placed a Ku Klux Klan hood on a controversial statue of the 19th Century colonialist Cecil Rhodes at Oriel College.In response to the protest, the college said it was "committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so"."We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination," it said.It added that permitting the event "does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers".Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Oxford protest against talk by academic who made Arday plagiarism claim

title: Henry Nowak killer applies to appeal against conviction
description: Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was stabbed to death with a 21cm (8in) kirpan, a religious blade that Digwa said he carried as part of his Sikh
body: Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was stabbed to death with a 21cm (8in) kirpan, a religious blade that Digwa said he carried as part of his Sikh faith.Digwa, then 22, told police that Nowak had attacked and racially abused him, which led to him being handcuffed as he lay dying. The Court of Appeal ruling included a finding that Nowak had not threatened Digwa and Digwa was responsible for the first act of force by snatching Henry's phone. Digwa then filmed Nowak as he lay bleeding on the ground and the ruling noted that in the video, Nowak can be heard denying that he had racially abused him.The trial judge later found Digwa's claims of racism to be a lie and there was no evidence Nowak was racist.Digwa was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June with a minimum term of 21 years.One of the four grounds on which Digwa plans to challenge his murder conviction is that the trial judge wrongly excluded from evidence WhatsApp messages Nowak sent when he was about 13, which Digwa suggested displayed a history of racist language.The messages were found by police during their review of Nowak's phone but the judge ruled them irrelevant and inadmissible.Digwa is also seeking to appeal his conviction on the basis the jury should not have been told that police had secretly recorded him confessing to the stabbing. The recording, he argues, breaks evidence rules relating to such material.On 5 November, the Court of Appeal ruled that the trial judge had been right to calculate Digwa's minimum term from a starting point of 15 years as there had been no evidence he had planned to use the knife as a weapon. Had that been the case, the starting point under sentencing law for murder would have been 25 years.But the Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr said the final figure of 21 years had been too low because it understated Digwa's repeated use of the knife and the "deliberate cruelty, additional suffering and obstruction" that followed.She and two other senior judges ordered "a very significant uplift ... to reflect the use of the large kirpan alone" and extended the minimum term to 25 years.Digwa and his lawyers are seeking a review of how the judges reached that figure."The Court of Appeal upheld the sentencing judge's finding that Vickrum Singh Digwa had not taken the kirpan to the scene intending to commit an offence or intending to have it available for use as a weapon," his lawyers said in a statement."The court nevertheless concluded that the circumstances surrounding the weapon justified a very significant uplift and ultimately substituted a 25-year minimum term."The application therefore raises an issue of wider importance."The Supreme Court reviews relatively few criminal cases and only does so where a point of law is disputed and it has wider implications for other cases.

schema.headline: Henry Nowak killer applies to appeal against conviction

title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it not reinstating Huang
description: "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a Tuesday call with financial analysts. The company's profits also
body: "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a Tuesday call with financial analysts. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter. Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader."The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout happening throughout the technology industry."It is business as usual," she said of what is happening inside of Nvidia now. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects"."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analyst questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement. Jones said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection."With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

schema.headline: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it not reinstating Huang

title: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
description: President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about
body: President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated. The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent."I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.  He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator in indirect talks with the US, was similarly dismissive of the CNN report."Same false flags, same war mongering, new logos," he posted on X.Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."  "Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added. Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb."But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now." It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to ​spy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

schema.headline: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington

title: Thomas Markle charged over child sex material in Philippines
description: Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child se
body: Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.Earlier this month, the 82-year-old was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.Markle, who is in custody, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney in the US for comment.Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor. Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

schema.headline: Thomas Markle charged over child sex material in Philippines
